newsitem.title: GERMANY: Koebnick sees 6-8 EMU members as best solution.
newsitem.headline: Koebnick sees 6-8 EMU members as best solution.

text.p: Bundesbank council member Hans-Juergen Koebnick said on Wednesday the "best solution" to the problems surrounding the start of European monetary union would be a punctual start with a medium-sized group.

"I still regard it as the best solution if EMU could start in 1999, initially with a core of six to eight countries whose currencies have in the past proven a high degree of internal and external stability and also do so for the future," he told a news conference.
"That would be the best way to transfer the confidence of the mark to the euro," he added.
But he added, "The current degree to which the Maastricht criteria have been fulfilled appears to stand in the way of such a largely risk-free solution."
Koebnick said he believed a punctual start would take precedence over exact adherence to the entry criteria.
"I tend to favour a punctual start and accept...that we (Germany) would not be a good fulfiller of the criteria, that we would require leeway in interpretation."

He said it would be more than embarrassing if Germany missed the deficit criteria. "Germany's voice would lose weight in future if we had to depend on other countries with a lesser tradition of stability to help us participate through a generous interpretation of the Treaty."
He added however that arguments such as the cost of German unification and Bonn's position as a net contributor in the European Union could help Germany's bid to join EMU.
Koebnick also said that concentrating on the need for sustainability of the criteria may lead to a differentiation between how Italy, Spain and Portugal are judged.
"It could be sensible that the three do not all join at the same time, but all are likely to be in monetary union by 2002," he said.
